cards.title: Modelling vortex interactions reveals distinct patterns of brain reconfiguration following psilocybin and escitalopram
cards.post: Aim: Determine how psilocybin and escitalopram reshape brain dynamics in depression, and whether vortex-space modelling captures treatment effects better than signal-space modelling. Methods: Pre- and post-treatment resting-state fMRI from a double-blind randomised controlled trial of psilocybin versus escitalopram in depression, compared using signal-space and vortex-space whole-brain models. Results: Vortex-space modelling was more sensitive than signal-space modelling in most analyses. Psilocybin increased vortex-space effective connectivity and reduced modularity, whereas escitalopram showed no comparable change. Greater increases in brain turbulence were associated with symptom reduction in both treatments. Conclusion: The two treatments reorganise brain dynamics in markedly different ways yet share features linked to clinical improvement, and vortex-space modelling is a promising framework for depression.
cards.why_you: Whole-brain modelling of treatment-induced dynamics in depression, directly relevant to your interest in neurodynamics and psychedelic treatment.

cards.title: Psilocybin induces delayed and dynamic changes in human sleep neurophysiology: Results from a randomized controlled trial of psilocybin assisted therapy in patients with comorbid major depressive and alcohol use disorder
cards.post: Aim: Characterise the acute and post-acute temporal dynamics of sleep neurophysiology after psilocybin-assisted therapy in comorbid depression and alcohol use disorder. Methods: Randomised placebo-controlled trial with 40 participants (psilocybin n=22, placebo n=18), home sleep EEG for three nights before and seven nights after administration, analysed with nonlinear mixed-effects models. Results: Delayed, nonlinear changes emerged after psilocybin, with NREM slow-wave activity, sigma and REM beta peaking or troughing around 3–4 nights post-administration. Sleep efficiency and total sleep time increased over the first three post-treatment nights, while architecture changes were largely absent. Conclusion: Psilocybin-assisted therapy induces delayed, dynamic sleep EEG changes beyond the acute period, suggesting sleep EEG may be a sensitive measure of evolving neurophysiology.
cards.why_you: Home EEG tracking of delayed neurophysiological effects after psilocybin links directly to your EEG and psychedelic clinical pharmacology work.

cards.title: Psychedelics and Sleep: Preclinical and Human Studies-A Systematic Review.
cards.post: Aim: To review preclinical and human evidence on how classic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, DMT/ayahuasca) alter sleep architecture, sleep quality, EEG activity and dreams. Methods: PRISMA-guided systematic review of PubMed up to May 2026; twelve eligible preclinical and clinical studies, with validity assessed by appropriate quality tools. Results: Preclinical studies consistently showed acute REM suppression, delayed REM onset and increased wakefulness. Human findings were heterogeneous: psilocybin prolonged REM latency, ayahuasca reduced REM duration, and slow-wave activity results were mixed. Conclusion: Classic psychedelics cause acute but transient sleep changes, mainly in REM sleep. Whether these contribute to therapeutic effects is uncertain, and the review was not prospectively registered.
cards.why_you: Your work on psychedelic clinical pharmacology and EEG markers makes the REM and slow-wave findings directly relevant to psilocybin and DMT studies.

cards.title: Reconsidering the Psychotomimetic Properties of LSD: Connectome-Based Classification Reveals Partial Overlap with First Episode Psychosis
cards.post: Aim: Compare the acute effects of LSD with medication-naive first episode psychosis on resting-state functional connectivity using connectome-based classification. Methods: Connectome-based classifiers trained separately on LSD versus placebo and on first episode psychosis versus healthy controls, with the LSD classifier validated externally and cross-applied between datasets. Results: Cross-application revealed partial overlap between LSD and psychosis, particularly involving the dorsal attention and sensorimotor networks. Univariate analysis supported between-network dysconnectivity in these networks as a point of convergence. Conclusion: Neural correlates of first episode psychosis partly overlap with LSD-induced changes, suggesting a possible serotonergic contribution, and direct comparative studies are needed.
cards.why_you: Compares LSD and psychosis connectivity with classification methods, close to your interests in psychedelic neuroscience and computational psychiatry.

cards.title: Psychedelic experience intensity during ketamine treatment and antidepressant outcomes.
cards.post: Aim: Test whether subjective psychedelic intensity during ketamine treatment is associated with antidepressant outcomes beyond an adverse-event framing. Methods: Retrospective longitudinal cohort of 3,637 adults with moderate-to-severe depression receiving up to four sublingual ketamine doses over four weeks, with subjective effects measured by the five-item Mindbloom Psychedelic Intensity scale at midpoint. Results: Higher intensity scores at two weeks were associated with greater PHQ-9 reduction at four weeks, higher likelihood of clinically significant change, and greater membership of an improvement trajectory, independent of dose and covariates. Conclusion: Subjective intensity of the ketamine experience is robustly associated with antidepressant response, although the retrospective design limits causal inference.
cards.why_you: Links subjective ketamine effects to treatment response, relevant to your work on ketamine and psychedelics as neuroplastogens in depression.

cards.title: From antidepressants to psychedelics: revisiting the pharmacology of so-called serotoninergic treatments
cards.post: Aim: Revisit the molecular mechanisms of antidepressants and OCD drugs to question whether SERT inhibition alone explains SSRI effects and psychedelic action. Methods: Narrative pharmacological review of the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of SSRIs and serotoninergic psychedelics, with focus on TrkB as a putative secondary target. Results: SSRI dosing needed for depression and OCD is consistent with a major target of much lower SSRI affinity than SERT, such as TrkB, which may offer a unifying account of antidepressant effects. Conclusion: TrkB may provide a unifying framework for antidepressant action, with implications for the therapeutic potential of psychedelics.
cards.why_you: Offers a molecular framework for psychedelic and SSRI mechanisms that bears on your computational chemistry and psychedelic pharmacology interests.

cards.title: Tracking single neurons across days reveals acute and persistent effects of psilocybin in the mouse brain
cards.post: Aim: Whether psilocybin's effects on single-neuron firing extend beyond the acute drug presence, and how acute responses relate to lasting changes. Methods: Chronically implanted Neuropixels probes in mice tracked 1,692 neurons in prefrontal and hippocampal regions after saline and psilocybin injections and again 24 h later. Results: Psilocybin bidirectionally modulated firing acutely in a cell-type and region-specific manner. Firing 24 h post-injection was net suppressed relative to saline, including in acutely activated neurons, and the late acute response predicted later firing. Conclusion: The authors present the first direct evidence of psilocybin's sustained effects on neuronal firing, offering insight into circuitry behind its lasting alterations.
cards.why_you: Directly relevant to your psilocybin work and to the link between acute drug effects and lasting neuroplasticity you study with PET and EEG.

cards.title: Feasibility of Simulated Low-Count [18F]FDG PET/MR for Patients with Pediatric Epilepsy.
cards.post: Aim: To test whether simulated low-count [18F]FDG PET/MR preserves diagnostic quality and epileptogenic zone lateralisation in paediatric epilepsy. Methods: Twenty-seven paediatric patients with epilepsy; list-mode data truncated to simulate 50%, 65% and 80% count reductions, analysed with ROI- and voxel-based lateralisation methods. Results: Contrast-to-noise fell and coefficient of variation rose with count reduction. Image quality stayed clinically acceptable up to 65% reduction, with consistent SUVRs and unchanged lateralisation agreement with the clinical consensus. Conclusion: A 65% simulated count reduction preserved acceptable image quality and lateralisation in paediatric epilepsy, supporting future lower-activity validation studies.
cards.why_you: Low-dose PET design and [18F]FDG quantification are close to your PET kinetic modelling and PET-MR methods work.

cards.title: OPM-MEG is characterized by increased sensitivity for visual gamma-band oscillations: A parallel EEG/OPM-MEG study
cards.post: Aim: Whether OPM-MEG detects visually induced gamma-band oscillations with higher sensitivity than EEG. Methods: Simultaneous EEG and OPM-MEG recordings in 26 participants during a visual grating task; gamma (30–80 Hz) and alpha/beta power and inter-trial phase coherence compared across modalities, with effect sizes as Cohen's dz. Results: OPM-MEG showed significantly higher SNR for visually induced gamma responses than EEG (dz = 0.97), seen in most participants with higher split-half correlations (EEG 0.88; OPM-MEG 0.94). Alpha/beta changes and ITPC showed no consistent modality difference. Conclusion: OPM-MEG offers enhanced sensitivity for visual gamma oscillations relative to EEG, which may support more precise study of cortical circuit function.
cards.why_you: Bears on your interest in EEG and MEG methods and in gamma-band dynamics for neurodynamics work.

cards.title: Selective distal upper extremity recovery following targeted dentate nucleus temporal interference stimulation in stroke-double-blind, sham-controlled randomized controlled trial with resting-state EEG
cards.post: Aim: Whether dentate nucleus-targeted temporal interference stimulation improves upper limb recovery after subacute stroke, with resting-state EEG as the main neurophysiological outcome. Methods: Double-blind, sham-controlled randomised trial in 50 subacute stroke patients (47 completers), 10 sessions of active or sham tTIS combined with standard rehabilitation; primary outcomes FMA-UE and ARAT. Results: Active stimulation improved FMA-UE (adjusted mean difference 3.98, d = 0.85, p = 0.006) and ARAT (2.98, d = 1.01, p = 0.005), driven by distal control. Active participants showed increased global beta and ipsilateral frontal theta power; no safety problems occurred. Conclusion: DN-targeted tTIS was safe and feasible and produced short-term distal upper limb gains, with EEG changes that the authors report as exploratory.
cards.why_you: Links deep-brain non-invasive stimulation and resting-state EEG spectral power, both close to your TMS-EEG and neurodynamics interests.

cards.title: Characterizing source-level electroencephalography activities to single-pulse TMS-EEG.
cards.venue: Clinical neurophysiology : official journal of the International Federation of Clinical Neurophysiology
cards.post: Aim: Whether source-level EEG measures distinguish active from sham single-pulse TMS over the left DLPFC at early and late latencies. Methods: Thirty-three healthy adults underwent active and sham TMS-EEG; analyses included TEPs, electric-field simulations, source-level SCD and SCS in target ROIs, whole-brain cluster permutation tests, and peripheral covariate adjustment after ICA. Results: Active stimulation gave larger early local TEPs (2.15 vs 0.85 μV) and greater target-region SCS and SCD in both windows. Significant whole-brain clusters appeared only at late latencies (about 270–375 ms), and one SCD cluster did not survive muscle-related adjustment. Conclusion: Target-region source measures separated active from sham stimulation, but late-stage whole-brain evidence needs cautious interpretation.
cards.why_you: Directly on TMS-EEG source analysis, a method you want to learn and that fits your interest in cortical excitability.

cards.title: Mechanism-aligned ketamine therapy for treatment-resistant depression: a 2026 update—toward an integrative mechanistic framework for clinical translation
cards.post: Aim: Propose an integrative mechanistic framework for ketamine therapy in treatment-resistant depression, updating a 2021 systems-level model with literature through April 2026. Methods: Narrative review integrating evidence on NMDAR modulation, neuroplastogenesis, anti-inflammatory signalling, entropic brain states and psychedelic phenomenology, with attention to chronic stress and attachment as cross-cutting factors. Results: The review synthesises five interacting domains proposed to underlie rapid ketamine effects and considers how developmental and relational factors may shape treatment resistance across depression, PTSD and suicidality. Conclusion: The framework aims to generate testable predictions about patient selection, timing and durability of ketamine response, pending controlled evaluation.
cards.why_you: Covers ketamine mechanisms with an entropic brain state component, relevant to your ketamine neuroplastogen and neurodynamics research.

cards.title: Difference in Patterns of Polysubstance Use Between Adults With Primary Cocaine Versus Methamphetamine Use Disorder: Findings From NIDA CTN-0108 Study.
cards.post: Aim: How demographics and polysubstance use patterns differ between people with primary cocaine and methamphetamine use disorders screened for a TMS trial. Methods: Screening data from 320 participants in NIDA CTN-0108 (120 with cocaine use disorder, 200 with methamphetamine use disorder), comparing demographics and substance use patterns. Results: Alcohol use was more prevalent in the cocaine group (67.9% vs 50%, p = 0.048) and cannabis use was similar (50.9% vs 46.1%). Polysubstance use remained common despite exclusion of moderate-to-severe comorbid SUDs. Conclusion: Polysubstance use persists in stimulant use disorder even under strict trial criteria, indicating a complex clinical profile that trial design should account for.
cards.why_you: Relevant to trial design for stimulant use disorder and to the clinical populations your psychedelic and neuromodulation work may later target.

cards.title: Connectome Harmonic Analysis at 7 Tesla Reveals Selective Reorganization of Large-Scale Cortical Dynamics in Adult Users of Cannabis.
cards.post: Aim: Whether cannabis use alters large-scale brain organisation, tested as changes in low-frequency connectome harmonics using 7T resting-state fMRI. Methods: Human Connectome Project 7T data from 81 cannabis users and 81 matched non-users; BOLD activity projected onto the first 200 connectome harmonics; t-tests with FDR correction and atlas localisation. Results: Cannabis users showed significantly greater power in one low-frequency harmonic (k = 6; t ≈ 4.19; p_FDR = 7.21 × 10⁻³; d = 0.659), roughly 44% higher than non-users, localised to a frontoparietal–sensorimotor network. It did not correlate with cannabis exposure variables, and behavioural associations did not survive FDR correction. Conclusion: Cannabis use is associated with selective amplification of one frontoparietal–sensorimotor eigenmode. The authors note the behavioural findings are nominal only.
cards.why_you: Connectome harmonics offer a macroscale eigenmode lens that complements your work on neurodynamics and whole-brain models.

cards.title: Bergenin ameliorates anxiety- and depression-like behavior in antibiotic-treated mice: behavioral and in silico insights.
cards.post: Aim: Whether bergenin, an anti-inflammatory isocoumarin, reverses anxiety- and depression-like behaviour induced by antibiotic-driven gut dysbiosis in mice. Methods: Antibiotic regimen in Swiss albino mice followed by 14 days of bergenin (25 or 50 mg/kg/day) or fluoxetine; elevated plus maze, open field, forced swim and tail suspension tests; docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics against TLR4-MD-2 and SERT. Results: Bergenin dose-dependently attenuated anxiety- and depression-like deficits, with high-dose recovery of about 70-92%, without altering behaviour in antibiotic-free animals. In silico, it bound the SERT S1 site with stability resembling fluoxetine, but its TLR4-MD-2 interaction was shallow. Conclusion: Bergenin ameliorates behavioural deficits in antibiotic-treated mice, and in silico data favour serotonergic over TLR4 involvement. The authors stress that the work is hypothesis-generating and that microbiome and mechanistic assays were not performed.
cards.why_you: Gut-brain and serotonergic mechanisms in mood fit your interest in brain-body coupling, though the link is indirect.

cards.title: The Potency Stability Tradeoff: Evaluating EEG Biomarkers for Major Depressive Disorder.
cards.post: Aim: Whether EEG biomarkers for major depressive disorder that are stable across data subsets generalise better than those with the strongest predictive signal. Methods: EEG from 30 MDD patients and 88 controls; connectivity, spectral and complexity features; XGBoost pipeline with leakage-free cross-validation and a nested Stability-Optimized Consensus Learning framework. Results: Theta and alpha features gave the strongest signal (max AUC 0.683) but were unstable across subsets (mean Jaccard 0.187) and overfitted. A model built on stable consensus biomarkers generalised better (AUC 0.792 vs 0.662) with less overfitting (P < .05). Conclusion: The MDD signature exists as a potent but unstable theta-alpha signal and a weaker but stable connectome signal. The authors argue stability matters more than strength for clinical biomarkers.
cards.why_you: Speaks to the reliability of EEG markers in depression, a question central to your EEG and computational psychiatry work.

cards.title: Bridging Treatment Gaps in Adolescent Depression With Neuromodulation Targeting Anhedonia
cards.post: Aim: Whether individualised functional connectivity-guided iTBS targeting left DLPFC improves depression and anhedonia in adolescents who have not responded to antidepressants. Methods: Commentary on a randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled trial of individualised iTBS in adolescents with major depressive disorder, with the target chosen by connectivity to the nucleus accumbens. Results: Active iTBS produced greater improvement in depressive symptoms than sham, with notable reduction in anhedonia. Change in anhedonia statistically mediated a substantial proportion of the later antidepressant effect. Conclusion: The mediation finding does not establish anhedonia as the mechanism, but suggests reward-related symptoms may be a useful neuromodulation target.
cards.why_you: Connects TMS targeting, reward circuitry and anhedonia, all areas you work on in TMS-EEG and psychiatry.

cards.title: Spectral and complexity-based signatures of advanced concentration absorption meditation: A high-density EEG study of jhana
cards.post: Aim: To characterise spectral and entropy-based EEG signatures of each jhana state of advanced concentration absorption meditation and relate them to experience. Methods: High-density EEG in 20 advanced meditators across eight ACAM-J states, with a multidimensional battery of spectral and complexity measures and phenomenological ratings. Results: Widespread posterior-central reductions in oscillatory and aperiodic power, posterior aperiodic flattening, and rising entropy-based complexity. Complexity stayed elevated in the most minimal states, and between practitioners higher entropy accompanied visual and auditory content. Conclusion: ACAM-J is a non-pharmacological model state at the high-complexity end of altered consciousness, revealing a dissociation between neural complexity and experiential richness.
cards.why_you: Directly connects to your EEG complexity, aperiodic activity and interoception interests, using a meditation model of altered consciousness.

Widespread posterior-central reductions in oscillatory and aperiodic power, posterior aperiodic flattening, and rising entropy-based complexity. Complexity stayed elevated in the most minimal states, and between practitioners higher entropy accompanied visual and auditory content.
Conclusion
ACAM-J is a non-pharmacological model state at the high-complexity end of altered consciousness, revealing a dissociation between neural complexity and experiential richness.

cards.title: Connectome modulates critical brain dynamics across local and global scales
cards.post: Aim: How local near-criticality within brain regions interacts with global criticality when regions are coupled through a mouse connectome. Methods: Multiscale model with neural mass models tuned near the asynchronous-synchronous transition, coupled via an empirical mouse connectome, plus whole-brain simulations of connectome-coupled spiking neurons. Results: Local criticality was modulated by long-range coupling, producing nonlinear timescale gradients. Global criticality, with scale-free avalanches and optimal functional connectivity, emerged only when local populations were near criticality and coupled within an optimal range. Conclusion: Local and global criticality are dynamically intertwined but not directly aligned, and their relationship depends on structural connectivity.
cards.why_you: A direct fit for your interests in criticality, neural mass and whole-brain modelling.

cards.title: The diastole-systole transition as a regulatory window for heart-brain coupling in major depressive disorder: Evidence from cardiac phase-dependent 1/f slope and periodic neural dynamics.
cards.post: Aim: Whether cardiac phase modulates periodic and aperiodic MEG activity differently in major depressive disorder. Methods: Simultaneous resting MEG and ECG in 60 patients and 60 matched controls, with a 6-month follow-up; SPRiNT separation of periodic and aperiodic activity; linear mixed models and permutation statistics. Results: Patients showed attenuated diastole-to-systole steepening of the left insular 1/f slope and greater late-systole delta reduction in the left anterior cingulate. Earlier posterior cingulate alpha peaks were also seen. Longitudinal insular changes in remitters were exploratory. Conclusion: Depression disrupts cardiac-cycle-dependent neural dynamics, with altered insular aperiodic modulation possibly reflecting excitation-inhibition and heart-brain synchrony changes.
cards.why_you: Combines heart-brain coupling, aperiodic 1/f analysis and MEG, three of your core interests.

cards.title: Interoceptive aberrations in major depressive disorder: Neural mechanisms, clinical correlates, and targeted interventions
cards.post: Aim: How interoceptive accuracy, sensibility and awareness are altered in major depressive disorder, and which neural mechanisms and interventions are involved. Methods: Narrative review comparing interoception assessment methods and synthesising behavioural, neurobiological and clinical findings, interpreted through an active-inference framework. Results: Interoceptive dysfunction in MDD is multidimensional, varying across task performance, bodily appraisal, metacognitive calibration and neural processing. Default mode network activity differs by illness stage, lower in early-stage and higher in chronic-stage samples. Conclusion: Measurement differences and illness stage likely explain inconsistent findings, and selected interoceptive processes may be modifiable, supporting mechanism-based testing in MDD.

cards.title: The Association between Physical Activity and Higher Corticolimbic Synaptic Density is Independent of Body Mass Index.
cards.venue: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
cards.post: Aim: Whether physical activity is associated with higher synaptic density in corticolimbic regions of the living human brain. Methods: PET with [18F]SynVesT-1 in 51 individuals (61% female), grouped as physically active or insufficiently active; group comparisons, regression and mediation analyses including BMI and depressive symptoms. Results: Physically active participants had higher synaptic density across corticolimbic regions (F6,44 = 2.41, p = 0.042), remaining marginal after adjusting for BMI and depressive symptoms (p = 0.050). Region-specific associations were positive, and BMI did not mediate the relationships. Conclusion: Physical activity is associated with higher synaptic density, particularly in prefrontal circuits, partly independent of BMI. Longitudinal studies are needed to establish causality.
cards.why_you: Directly relevant to your synaptic density PET work with [11C]UCB-J, here using the SV2A-alternative tracer in a neuroplasticity context.

cards.title: Animal models in psychedelic research - Tripping over translation.
cards.post: Aim: To audit how rodent psychedelic studies are designed and whether their conditions and assays could translate to human therapy. Methods: Systematic review of 266 rodent psychedelic studies published 2014 to 2026, assessing welfare and set-and-setting-like factors, behavioural assay design, and individual and social factors. Results: Most studies included stress-inducing factors: only 14% tested in the active phase, 7% used environmental enrichment, and 21% used refined handling. Drug administration almost universally used restraint-requiring methods. Most assays were brief and isolated, and group-level cross-sectional designs dominated. Conclusion: The authors argue translation requires longitudinal tracking of individuals in enriched social settings with comprehensive behavioural characterisation.
cards.why_you: Directly relevant to your psychedelic clinical pharmacology and preclinical translation questions, including how set and setting shape human outcomes.

cards.title: Psychedelics shift decision strategies and reconfigure orbitofrontal dynamics.
cards.post: Aim: Determine how psilocybin and ketamine reshape perceptual decision-making and orbitofrontal population dynamics in mice. Methods: Mice trained on a free-response perceptual decision task disentangling bias from sensory strategies, given acute psilocybin or ketamine, analysed with drift diffusion, GLM-HMM, whole-brain c-Fos mapping and OFC calcium imaging. Results: Both drugs slowed decisions and improved accuracy via higher decision thresholds and a shift toward sensory-engaged states. OFC population dynamics were reorganised, with preserved task selectivity but altered temporal structure and population correlations. Conclusion: Psychedelics shift decision-making toward greater reliance on sensory evidence while reshaping cortical population dynamics.
cards.why_you: Population dynamics and behavioural modelling of psychedelic effects connect to your neurodynamics work and interest in psychedelic mechanisms.

cards.title: Reference-region normalization outperforms data-driven approaches in [18F]FDG PET of dementia with Lewy bodies.
cards.post: Aim: To compare intensity normalisation methods for [18F]FDG PET in dementia with Lewy bodies, identifying the most suitable approach. Methods: [18F]FDG PET/MR in 110 DLB patients and 30 controls; reference-region, proportional scaling, iterative and histogram-based methods compared on normative alignment, disease independence, stability and simulated phantom recovery. Results: Reference-region normalisation gave smaller DLB-control scaling differences, weaker meta-ROI correlations and lower variability than data-driven methods. The white matter and pons had the highest composite scores. Conclusion: Reference-region normalisation is preferred in DLB, outperforming proportional scaling, histogram and data-driven approaches in this large cohort.
cards.why_you: Directly relevant to your [18F]FDG and PET quantification work, offering a benchmark for normalisation choices in your own protocols.

cards.title: Revisiting entropy and entropy-related magnitudes of a symbolic sequence and their estimation.
cards.post: Aim: To revisit entropy, entropy density, effective measure complexity and informational distance, and how to estimate them for sequential data. Methods: Theoretical review linking Shannon entropy and Kolmogorov complexity, with estimation via Lempel-Ziv factorisation and an open-source parallel software library; three case studies on fMRI, coupled oscillators and ECG. Results: Ziv's theorem gives asymptotic equivalence between normalised distinct-word counts and entropy density, supporting estimation of these measures for finite sequences. Case studies illustrate applications to brain connectivity, oscillator dynamics and atrial fibrillation classification. Conclusion: The framework captures structural and dynamical properties across domains, with practical estimation tools for finite data.
cards.why_you: Strongly tied to your EEG complexity and information-theoretic neurodynamics work, and offers a ready estimation library for Lempel-Ziv measures.

cards.title: MLE EEG Toolbox: A Personal AI Laboratory Assistant for Literature-Informed and Reproducible M/EEG Research
cards.post: Aim: To build a locally run AI assistant that links methodological literature, natural-language instructions and reproducible EEG and MEG analysis. Methods: Software framework combining a constrained local language model, literature retrieval, provenance tracking and cross-platform tests, applied to public EEG and MEG datasets. Results: Action-selection accuracy was 85.6% for EEG and 95.5% for MEG. 142 cross-platform tests showed close numerical agreement. Spectral, network, decoding and source analyses were demonstrated on public data. Conclusion: The toolbox offers a researcher-controlled, reproducible environment running on standard personal computers without external AI APIs.
cards.why_you: Relevant to your EEG and MEG analysis workflows and reproducibility, and could reduce friction in your neurodynamics pipelines.

cards.title: An engineered nanobody inhibitor for molecular-to-circuit control of opioid receptors
cards.post: Aim: Whether an engineered intracellular nanobody can selectively inhibit active opioid receptors and control their signalling in defined cells. Methods: Structure-guided evolution of intracellular nanobodies, functional optimisation, and testing in cells, VTA neurons and mice, including cell-type-specific expression in VTA GABAergic neurons with fentanyl challenge. Results: Nb64 rapidly suppressed transducer engagement, receptor internalisation and μOR-driven GIRK currents. Cell-type-specific expression attenuated fentanyl-evoked dopamine release and behavioural responses. Conclusion: Nb64 offers a general strategy for precise in vivo inhibition of native GPCR signalling, though its use across other settings remains to be established.
cards.why_you: Relevant to your interest in opioid and reward circuitry and in tools for dissecting receptor signalling in VTA and dopamine systems.

cards.title: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts.
cards.post: Aim: To identify the molecular signal that draws cannibalistic locusts to injured conspecifics. Methods: Behavioural assays, olfactory receptor knockdowns, and bacterial gene-cluster deletions in Locusta migratoria, examining the symbiont-derived volatile guaiacol. Results: Guaiacol, released more after injury, attracts nymphs and triggers cannibalism via receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34. It is made by the symbiont Enterobacter hormaechei; deleting its gene cluster abolished production and behavioural effects. At low levels it activates immune pathways. Conclusion: A microbial-chemical signal links immune defence with cannibalism, offering molecular targets for population manipulation.
cards.why_you: Only loosely relevant to your work; a neuroscientist might find the olfactory-receptor-to-behaviour mapping an interesting model of chemical signalling.

cards.title: The fate of poised pre-mRNAs shapes mitochondrial activity and cellular differentiation.
cards.post: Aim: To determine how nuclear RNA quality control decides the fate of poised intron-containing polyadenylated pre-mRNAs. Methods: Molecular and genetic study in mouse and human cells, including NCBP3 depletion and pathogenic RNA exosome mutations, with analysis of mitochondrial function and motor behaviour. Results: NCBP3 favours splicing of poised pre-mRNAs while anillin favours exosome degradation; many affected transcripts encode mitochondrial factors. NCBP3 loss or exosome mutations reduced mitochondrial activity, causing muscle weakness, cerebellar hypomyelination and poorer motor coordination. Conclusion: A competition between pre-mRNA pathways controls mitochondrial function, and its disruption contributes to neurological disease.
cards.why_you: Only loosely relevant to your fields; a neuroscientist might find the link between mitochondrial gene regulation and cerebellar disease of interest.

cards.title: A glucose-powered artificial neuroimmune axis for metabolic control.
cards.post: Aim: Whether a battery-free, glucose-powered artificial neuroimmune axis can restore metabolic and immune balance through closed-loop vagal-like stimulation. Methods: NeuroAxis, a closed-loop device powered by endogenous glucose with metabolic interoceptive feedback, tested in rat models of type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Results: NeuroAxis supported recovery of β-cells and reduced inflammation in type 1 diabetes rats, drove macrophage remodelling in type 2 diabetes rats, and restored glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity in both, with effects persisting after treatment. Conclusion: The authors propose NeuroAxis as a general approach for autonomous interorgan regulation, based on rodent models.
cards.why_you: Interoceptive feedback loops and autonomic control are adjacent to your brain–body coupling interests, though the work is outside your neuroscience focus.

cards.title: A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke's area.
cards.post: Aim: Does Wernicke's area, classically linked to speech comprehension, also contribute to generating speech, and if so, what does it encode? Methods: Direct intracranial recordings in human patients, cortical stimulation and lesion analysis, examining activity before speech and causal necessity for production. Results: A discrete subzone, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus, activates before speech, is causally necessary for production, and encodes features of whole upcoming words rather than low-level acoustics or articulation. Its activity differs from nearby auditory-feedback responses and can decode intended speech in people with paralysis. Conclusion: Wernicke's area contains a dedicated subregion for speech generation alongside its role in auditory processing.
cards.why_you: Adds a causal human-cortex perspective on how a region's perceptual role coexists with production, relevant to your interest in neurodynamics and whole-brain organisation.

cards.title: A Single Dose of Psilocybin Increases Synaptic Density and Decreases 5-HT2A Receptor Density in the Pig Brain
cards.post: Aim: To test whether a single psilocybin dose changes synaptic density (SV2A) and 5-HT2A receptor density in the pig brain. Methods: Twenty-four awake pigs received psilocybin 0.08 mg/kg or saline intravenously and were euthanised at one or seven days. Autoradiography of hippocampus and prefrontal cortex used [3H]UCB-J, [3H]MDL100907 and [3H]Cimbi-36. Results: One day after psilocybin, hippocampal SV2A density was 4.42% higher and 5-HT2A density was lower in hippocampus and prefrontal cortex (−15.21% to −50.19%), significant for hippocampus across ligands and for prefrontal cortex with Cimbi-36 only. At seven days SV2A remained higher (+9.24% hippocampus, +6.10% prefrontal cortex), with no 5-HT2A differences. Conclusion: Psilocybin may cause persistent synaptogenesis and an acute fall in 5-HT2A density, possibly contributing to antidepressant effects.
cards.why_you: Directly relevant to your synaptic density PET ([11C]UCB-J) and 5-HT2A work, providing a preclinical benchmark for psilocybin plasticity.

cards.title: Cortical dynamics during psychedelic and anesthetized states induced by ketamine
cards.post: Aim: To characterise how the spatiotemporal complexity of EEG activity changes across subanesthetic and anaesthetic doses of ketamine. Methods: High-density scalp EEG in healthy volunteers during subanesthetic and anaesthetic ketamine. Hidden Markov modelling classified brain states, and Lempel-Ziv complexity was computed per state after controlling for spectral changes. Results: Subanesthetic ketamine raised complexity relative to baseline. Anaesthetic ketamine produced alternating low and high complexity before stabilising at a high level comparable to baseline. Conclusion: Ketamine-induced state transitions share features of anaesthesia, normal consciousness and altered consciousness, illustrating its complex pharmacological properties.
cards.why_you: Closely matches your ketamine EEG work and your interest in Lempel-Ziv complexity and criticality as markers of altered states.
